result: The study demonstrates a striking correspondence between BOLD signal changes and single-unit neuronal firing in two fusiform gyrus regions: lateral MidFG (P1) showed increased BOLD and increased neuronal firing to faces, while medial MidFG (P2) showed decreased BOLD and decreased neuronal firing to faces. This indicates that BOLD decreases can reflect spike suppression in human association cortex.
evaluation: Reviewers acknowledged this as an important observation but expressed concern about the study design. One reviewer noted 'the observation of positive BOLD and neuronal activation is made at one brain site in one patient, while the complementary observation of negative BOLD and neuronal suppression actually derives from the other patient. Showing both effects in both patients would make a much stronger paper.' Another reviewer raised concerns about the SSVEP paradigm lacking a true baseline, making it difficult to distinguish between lower firing rates versus genuine suppression.

result: About one-third (34.3%) of neurons in the medial MidFG showing reduced firing to faces lacked a significant general visual response, indicating genuine suppression of baseline spiking activity upon face presentation rather than merely relative reduction compared to objects.
evaluation: Reviewers found this claim critical but insufficiently supported. One reviewer stated 'The authors report that ~30% of neurons showed absolute suppression, but those data are not shown separately from the neurons that only show relative reductions. It is difficult to evaluate the absolute suppression claim from the short assertion in the text alone.' Another reviewer questioned the interpretation, noting 'because the experiment does not have a true baseline (e.g. blank screen, with no visual stimulation) this experimental design cannot distinguish between lower firing rate to faces vs suppression of response to faces.'

result: Using frequency-tagging paradigms, the study found robust face-selective differential activity in both fMRI and electrophysiology, with very high proportions of face-selective neurons in both activated (P1: 86.5-98.1%) and deactivated (P2: 77.9-86.6%) MidFG regions, representing about 70% of neurons overall.
evaluation: Reviewers accepted the face-selectivity findings without challenge. One reviewer noted 'the methods used for comparing face and object responses in both fMRI and electrode recordings were robust and well-established.' The editor described the methods as 'solid' and the dataset as 'valuable' with 'potentially general importance.'

result: fMRI localization confirmed that faces elicited larger BOLD responses in lateral MidFG (P1) but lower BOLD responses in medial MidFG (P2), with microelectrode locations falling within these respective activation and deactivation regions.
evaluation: Reviewers did not question the fMRI localization findings. One reviewer summarized: 'The electrode location in one patient showed activation of the BOLD response and activation of neuronal firing in response to face stimuli...The other patient showed...a suppression of the BOLD response to face stimuli.' The anatomical correspondence was accepted as demonstrated.

result: The mean onset response latency did not differ between neuronal increases and decreases (118.2 ms vs. 127.3 ms, p > 0.05), but the absolute average firing rate was significantly lower for decreases than increases (−2.73 vs. 3.69 spikes/s, p < 0.01).
evaluation: Reviewers did not challenge these latency and firing rate comparisons. The findings were presented as supporting data for the main results and were not questioned in the reviews.

result: Across 245 units recorded (206 single-units, 39 multi-units) over multiple sessions, only a small proportion failed to respond (16.1% in P1, 11.8% in P2), with no significant differences between participants in response proportions or face-selectivity.
evaluation: Reviewers acknowledged the dataset as valuable. One reviewer noted 'The data is unique as it contains a lot of single and multiunit recordings (245 units) from the human fusiform gyrus.' Another stated 'These patient data are valuable, with many recording sessions and neurons from human face-selective regions.' The quantitative findings were not challenged.

result: Two epilepsy patients were implanted with hybrid macro-microelectrodes in fusiform gyrus: P1's electrodes were in lateral MidFG (FG4/FFA region), while P2's were in medial MidFG (FG3), representing an unprecedented sampling of a face-deactivated region.
evaluation: Reviewers accepted the experimental setup and patient characteristics. The editor described it as 'an ingenious use of clinical patient data' and reviewers noted the value of the recordings. One reviewer suggested highlighting the limitation that 'both effects' were not shown 'in both patients' but did not dispute the anatomical localization claims.

result: The contrasted pattern of BOLD activation/deactivation for faces in lateral/medial fusiform gyrus has been systematically observed across hemispheres, despite right hemisphere dominance in face recognition.
evaluation: Reviewers did not challenge this contextual claim about the broader literature. It was presented as established knowledge supported by citations and used to justify the study design.
